_about: Everything this catalogue asserted and later found to be wrong, kept as a row instead of a quiet edit. `was` is what it said before; `why` is what changed the answer.
_why: The README already lists errors inherited from the source data and leaves them visible on purpose. This is the same policy applied to the project's own output: a catalogue that silently corrects itself gives no way to judge how often it is wrong.

corrections.was: 2013 — Stomakhin, Schroeder, Chai, Teran & Selle, A material point method for snow simulation
corrections.now: 1994 — Sulsky, Chen & Schreyer, A particle method for history-dependent materials, CMAME 118, 179–196; Stomakhin et al. 2013 recorded as the graphics introduction
corrections.why: The catalogue dated the material point method to the SIGGRAPH paper that made it famous, nineteen years after the method was published. The mis-dating hid a lineage that runs through this very table: MPM was built as an extension of FLIP — already an entry here, dated 1986 — from fluids to solid mechanics, the addition being that each particle carries the full stress tensor so history-dependent materials become possible. Dating it 2013 severed a link the model exists to show.

corrections.was: 1974 — Finkel & Bentley, Quad trees: a data structure for retrieval on composite keys, Acta Informatica 4, 1–9
corrections.now: 1971 — Klinger for the region quadtree, the name from Hunter's 1978 thesis, the octree from Meagher 1980; Finkel & Bentley recorded as the point quadtree, a different structure
corrections.why: Two different structures share the name, and the catalogue cited the wrong one. Finkel and Bentley's quadtree splits at data points for retrieval on composite keys. The structure the entry actually describes — always split at the midpoint, subdivide only where there is detail — is the region quadtree, and it is the one graphics and generation use almost exclusively. Same word, different data structure, different paper, three years earlier.

Buck's Mazes for Programmers, which is the citation the entry already gives, dates Eller's algorithm to 1982. The catalogue's 1980 appears to have been an approximation to the decade rather than a read of the source it names.

corrections.was: 1993, linking to Wikipedia's fractional Brownian motion article
corrections.now: 1994, linking to the table of contents of the book the chapter is in
corrections.why: Two problems in one row. Texturing & Modeling: A Procedural Approach was first published in 1994, not 1993 — and for a citation whose whole point is that it is a book chapter rather than a paper, the year should be the book's. The URL pointed at the Wikipedia article for fBm, which is the thing ridged multifractal is a modification *of* and says nothing about the modification.
Found by checking all 125 citation URLs: handwiki.org times out on connect. It was also a mirror of the Wikipedia article it has been replaced with, so nothing is lost.

corrections.now: an Internet Archive snapshot of the same PDF
corrections.why: Also found by the URL sweep: the Yale host's TLS certificate no longer matches its own name, so the link fails for anything that validates certificates. The paper is the correct one and the archived copy is identical.

A source takes nothing but a seed and parameters. Curl noise takes the curl of a potential field built from noise, so something goes in — it cannot produce a flow field without a noise basis underneath it. Filed as a source, it claimed to be usable in place of Perlin or simplex noise rather than on top of one. Same correction as the concept-level one on `noise`, one layer down.

corrections.was: the date the registry lookup ran — 2022-05 or 2022-06 on 23 of 71 rows
corrections.now: the actual publish date of the recorded version, from the registry, ranging 2013 to 2026
corrections.why: The file itself had noticed the anomaly and explained it wrongly. Its caveat said the 2022 dates "cluster too tightly across unrelated projects to be real" and guessed at a bulk registry metadata operation, then advised the reader not to treat them as abandonment. Re-resolving showed the field had simply been filled with the check date. The advice was backwards: noisejs last shipped in 2013, csg and voronoi in 2015, markovchain in 2016, and the wrong dates were hiding exactly the abandonment the caveat told you to disregard.

corrections.was: the string "null" on 12 rows; the first 25 characters of the licence text on 3 more, e.g. "GNU General Public Licens"
corrections.now: SPDX identifiers, taken from license_expression where PyPI provides one
corrections.why: Two separate bugs in one field. Twelve rows carried the four-character string "null" rather than a null value, so a query for unlicensed packages returned nothing. Three others held truncated licence prose, because some PyPI projects paste their entire licence text into the metadata field and it had been cut to a fixed width. The whole column is now normalised to SPDX, so it can be filtered on.

corrections.was: "registry verification cannot reach GitHub-hosted C++ (FastNoiseLite, mxgmn's WFC, Recast, CGAL). That needs a different check."
corrections.now: resolved — the GitHub, crates.io and NuGet APIs are now used alongside npm and PyPI, and all four of those named libraries are recorded
corrections.why: The gap was a method limitation, not a real absence, and the README said so. Four registries were added: api.github.com/repos for the C++ and shader libraries that ship only as repositories, crates.io for Rust, and NuGet for C#. All four named examples are now rows, and the technologies table no longer has C++, Rust, C# and GLSL sitting empty.

corrections.was: "94 of 184 algorithms have no implementation recorded ... That is a worse ratio than before, and honestly so: 49 implementations were added and 59 algorithms, so the layer grew faster than its coverage."
corrections.now: The absolute gap grew because the denominator did. Coverage rose from 46 of 125 algorithms (36.8%) to 90 of 184 (48.9%), and concepts with no implementation fell from 13 of 28 to 10 of 36.
corrections.why: Written during the same pass that added the rows, and wrong. The uncovered *count* rose from 79 to 94, which is unavoidable when 59 algorithms are added, but the *ratio* improved in both directions. Worth keeping as a row rather than quietly fixing, because of where it was: the section of the README whose entire job is to stop the map looking more finished than it is. A claim of self-criticism that turns out to be arithmetically false is a worse failure there than an overclaim would be somewhere else — it buys credibility it has not earned. The tell was the phrase "grew faster than its coverage", which sounds like a measurement and is not one; nobody had divided.
